blocks.c: There is a song lamplighters teach their apprentices, and it is not a good song. It has no tune worth the name and its rhymes are the kind that only work if you are cold and it is late. It exists to be counted along with, one lamp to a line, so that a lighter walking a long round in the dark knows without thinking whether she has missed one.

One for the crossing and two for the well,
three for the door that they never will sell,
four for the corner, and five for the stair,
six for the lamp that was already there.

Ines had learned it at nine and had not thought about the sixth line since. Nobody did. It was the line you sang while fumbling with the ladder, and it meant nothing, and it had always meant nothing, and now she stood in the guildhall cellar with an oil measure in one hand thinking about it with an intensity that frightened her a little.
The archivist's explanation took the better part of an hour and required two cups of the terrible cellar tea.

Some lamps, she said, are lit by the district. Some lamps light the district. The second kind are older than the guild, older than the ledgers, older than the cobbles that gave up at the turn of the lane, and the guild's whole function — its ledgers, its oil, its grudges, its small meaningless circles — was to keep the second kind company so that they did not get bored and wander.
We do not maintain that lamp. We attend it. The distinction is the entire profession, and it is the reason we write everything down.
"Ah," said the archivist, and put her cup down. "Those are yours. You simply haven't made them yet."
